In black-box settings where gradients are inaccessible, existing methods tend to guess adversarial transformations using external knowledge, ignoring the information provided by the target model. To mitigate this, we propose a trainable black-box framework based on reinforcement learning, which learns from the target model to generate tailored adversarial transformations. We demonstrate that our approach achieves lower post-attack accuracy, greater query efficiency and better semantic preservation on both natural language inference and generative Q&A tasks. On natural language inference, it drives post-attack accuracy to 2% within 20 queries. Against generative language models, our trained attacker consistently achieves lower post-attack accuracy than the untrained attacker and wins in 4 out of 6 settings when compared to a strong optimization-based baseline. We further experiment with multiple reward designs and training settings, and we find that no design or setting is consistently dominant. Our code is available at this https URL .

papers.title: "A Space Where I Can Be Myself": Exploring Safe Visibility for Graduate Student Mothers in Mom Cafes
papers.abstract: Graduate student mothers navigate intertwined demands of graduate study and caregiving, yet little is known about how they seek support through online communities. We examine this through Mom Cafes, locally based online parenting communities in South Korea. Drawing on focus group interviews and design workshops with 22 graduate student mothers, we identify a pattern of dual invisibility: caregiving circumstances were difficult to make legible in academic contexts, while academic circumstances were difficult to make legible in parenting contexts. Although Mom Cafes offered useful local information and emotional reassurance, concerns specific to graduate student motherhood were harder to articulate or safely disclose. Participants sought ways to make graduate student motherhood recognizable when relevant, but their designs highlighted tensions around identifiability, judgment, relational burden and accountability. We conceptualize these tensions as safe visibility and discuss infrastructures for selective recognition, low-obligation connection, and accountable pathways to practical care.

papers.title: Levenshtein-type bounds for $(a,b)$-avoiding spherical codes
papers.abstract: We develop a Levenshtein-type linear programming framework (for maximal $s$-codes and for minimal energy) for $(a,b)$-avoiding spherical codes, that is, codes whose inner products between distinct points avoid $(a,b)$. We introduce and investigate signed measures that are positive definite up to an appropriate degree and yield stationary auxiliary linear programming polynomials and exact quadrature formulas. We give explicit conditions for positivity of the quadrature weights and sufficient Krein-type conditions for nonnegative Gegenbauer coefficients (positive definiteness of the candidate optimal linear programming polynomials). Under these hypotheses and suitable node-location assumptions, the resulting cardinality bounds are optimal within the corresponding degree restriction and unique under natural nondegeneracy conditions. Under proper conditions on the quadrature nodes, we obtain universal lower energy bounds by utilizing Hermite interpolants as polynomial solutions of the respective linear program. Common test functions characterize optimality in the full polynomial linear programs under mild additional assumptions.

papers.title: Optimal Feedback Control of the Fokker-Planck Equation for an SIRS Epidemic Model
papers.abstract: We develop a Fokker--Planck feedback control framework for a stochastic susceptible--infected--recovered--susceptible (SIRS) epidemic model with three intervention mechanisms targeting disease transmission, loss of immunity, and recovery. The interventions are formulated as space- and time-dependent feedback controls that influence both the drift and diffusion coefficients of the underlying stochastic differential equations, allowing control of the probability distribution of epidemic states. We investigate the existence of optimal controls and derive first-order necessary optimality conditions involving a forward Fokker--Planck equation, a backward adjoint equation, and a Hamiltonian minimization condition. For numerical approximation, we combine a Chang--Cooper discretization of the diagonal drift--diffusion terms with a finite-difference treatment of cross-diffusion and a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) algorithm for computing the optimal feedback policies. We also examine sufficient-decrease and convergence properties of the SQH iteration. Numerical experiments consider four epidemiological objectives involving cumulative infection burden, infection-threshold exceedance, terminal susceptible population, and a combination of running and terminal costs. The resulting feedback policies exhibit distinct spatial and temporal structures depending on the epidemiological objective. Monte Carlo simulations of the underlying stochastic system illustrate that the optimized interventions can substantially reduce infection growth and undesirable epidemic outcomes relative to uncontrolled dynamics. The proposed framework provides a distribution-based approach to stochastic epidemic control that integrates mathematical analysis, numerical optimization, and state-dependent intervention design.

papers.title: Measuring Bounded Autonomy for an LLM Decomposition Planner on a Live 5G-Core Testbed
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are entering network-management control loops, yet their plans can fall outside the executable action space. Whether hard deterministic bounds around such a planner have real effect, or merely restate a definition, is an empirical question. We measure it on a live 5G-core testbed, where an LLM planner decides when to decompose control-plane procedures into stateless handlers inside a bounded loop: a JSON schema constrains the output, a projection-repair validator re-checks it, a deterministic fallback guarantees liveness, and every decision is persisted. Three measurements anchor the paper. First, the two tested models, run unbounded with the allowed action sets stated in the prompt, still violated intent-handler rules in 13 of 44 standard calls. Every violation broke an intent-handler combination rule that the deployed flat schema cannot encode (schema enforcement as deployed caught 0/13); a union schema encoding the rule removes the class by construction. Second, with the bounds in place, all 33 decoded live plans were feasible without repair, and a matched-condition probe put the in-distribution unbounded rate at one violation in 20 windows. Third, exploratory: on the design set the planner matched an author-specified selection reference that a threshold policy and three a priori codings each missed. Transfer to held-out scenarios remained partial (5-6 of 10), and the planner's two-clause distillate could replace the runtime planner itself. Together, the results suggest elicitation and distillation, not runtime control, as the LLM's role.

papers.title: Dual-Stream LLM-Guided Reward Design for Reject-Inference-Aware Reinforcement Learning in E-Commerce Payment Fraud Detection
papers.abstract: Production fraud-detection models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic: transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels, so models train on a biased, approved-only distribution. We extend LLM-guided reward design, the framework of Qu et al. (2025) in which an LLM evolves the reward of a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, to attack this reject-inference problem inside the reward. A single LLM designs a dual-stream reward: stream 1 applies the standard dollar-weighted precision objective to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal against the legacy scores that drove the original block. Rather than prescribe which signals matter, we expose a superset of evidence and let the LLM decide for itself which to use, guided by evaluation feedback alone; because it writes the reward as code, that choice is directly auditable. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and the production baseline by +6.8 points on average. The resulting policy is architecturally identical to that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost.

papers.title: Faster Treasure Hunt via Strongly Universal Exploration with Polylogarithmic Overhead
papers.abstract: We study deterministic exploration and delayed-activation treasure hunt in anonymous undirected port-labeled graphs with incoming-port information. From polynomial-time constructible ordinary universal exploration sequences of length \(O(n^c)\) for a fixed regular degree, we construct a single infinite strongly universal exploration sequence with cover time \(O(n^c\log^2n)\). Summable dyadic insertion schedules yield the sharper bound \(O_\eps(n^c\log n(\log\log n)^{1+\eps})\) for every fixed \(\eps>0\), together with refinements at every fixed iterated-logarithm depth. The proof combines reversible excursions, neutral guards and an arbitrary-window argument that treats both orientations simultaneously. For this recurrence, uniform linear expansion is equivalent to convergence of the normalized period sum. Exact counting identities also permit direct instruction access. With a logspace ordinary generator, table-free enumeration of decreasing scale paths computes instruction \(t\) using \(O(\log(t+2))\) working bits and time polynomial in \(t\). The earlier polynomial-slack bounds follow as corollaries. A local cubic simulation extends the treasure-hunt application to arbitrary-degree graphs, with the \(2m\)-vertex replacement size included explicitly in the bound.

papers.title: Contextuality and Contradictions: Exploring Real-World Identifications of AI-Generated Writing
papers.abstract: As AI-generated content spreads into nearly every domain of human interaction, practices and discourses of AI detection, both formal and informal, have become an everyday part of how people interact with text and with each other. In this paper, we explore the real-world practices and discourses of AI identification that have emerged in response to a shifting discursive landscape where the human provenance of a text can no longer be taken for granted. We pair qualitative coding with computational analysis of lexical change, grounded in linguistic anthropological perspectives on language and communication, to investigate AI identifications among English Wikipedia editors and students. We find that these identifications draw on a diversity of evidentiary types, from discrete textual features and judgments about content to circular sense-making claims and presumptions about the author's moral character, and that they are contradictory, dynamic, and contextually dependent. In practice, what often motivates an AI identification is not the presence of any specific textual element, but pragmatic infelicity: a perceived mismatch between the elements present and those deemed appropriate within the text's particular context. Consequently, real-world identifications of AI-generated writing do not merely neutrally point out the perceived presence of "AI-like" features, but can be leveraged as a discursive resource to maintain and define sociolinguistic norms: what can be said in a given context, what is appropriate, and, ultimately, what is human. Further, the design and implementation of systems and tools that treat AI-likeness as a context-free property of text may therefore inherit, and enforce at scale, the norms of whichever contexts they were trained on.

papers.title: Foundation-Model Residuals as Signals of Urban Bus Irregularity
papers.abstract: Pretrained trajectory models encode mobility patterns learned across cities, but their errors when transferred to a new city are usually treated only as performance limitations. We instead ask whether these residuals reveal systematic local conditions. Architectures such as UniTraj and TrajFM learn transferable trajectory representations, although cross-context transfer remains challenging. Using the NetMob26 bus location, ticketing, weather, network, and socioeconomic data for Niteroi, we analyze spatial and travel-time residuals of these recent trajectory foundation models. We test whether high residuals concentrate spatially, whether spatial and travel-time residuals overlap, and which urban-context variables explain their distribution. We interpret high residuals as candidate proxy signals of transit irregularity rather than direct evidence of service disruption, and analyze their contextual associations using Explainable AI (XAI). Insights into such varied environments are increasingly valuable for evaluating new urban paradigms; for instance, the 15-minute-city perspective serves as a key motivation for our approach, guiding our methods and expanding the analysis beyond standard mobility metrics.

papers.title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics and galaxy clusters
papers.abstract: First proposed by Milgrom in 1983 as an alternative to the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) paradigm, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) has gained renewed momentum in light of persistent non-detections of exotic dark matter particles and growing tensions facing CDM on galactic scales. While MOND perfectly reproduces galactic rotation curves, it encounters notable challenges in explaining the equilibrium of galaxy clusters. Although it reduces the overall dark matter budget in these massive systems, an unidentified mass component remains required. This paper investigates the hypothesis that this missing mass is baryonic: composed of non-radiating ordinary matter such as stellar remnants, gas too diffuse to initiate star formation, or compact, ultra-dense clouds of cold molecular gas with low volume filling factors. Using a sample of 106 clusters mapped in X-rays, emitted by the hot intra-cluster medium (ICM) composing most of the visible mass, we derive first the total mass within the Newtonian dynamics, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. Then, with the modified Poisson equation, we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the invisible missing matter within the MOND framework. In the sample, the relaxed systems harboring cooling flows, known as cool-core clusters, have the highest peaks of dark missing mass. Its density profile reveals a pronounced central concentration bounded by a steep truncation immediately beyond a core radius of 20-30 kpc, confirming previous studies. MOND reduces the necessary dynamical mass by a factor of 4 to 10. The residual missing mass is proportional to the total gas mass, being roughly twice lower.

papers.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies
papers.abstract: Execution algorithms are calibrated asset by asset, because the queues, trade rates and bid-ask spreads they face differ by orders of magnitude across assets. For reinforcement learning this is zero-shot generalisation across contexts of very different scales, and microstructure invariance proposes a normalisation fixed by theory: measured in each asset's own units of time, size and price, markets look alike. In an exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data, we train policies once, on 954 stocks in 2019, to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, and evaluate them unchanged on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs and a second exchange. First, a policy that sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick) costs within 0.015 spreads per share (a fifth of what learning saves) of a policy whose training data included the stock, and the stock's own history does not help it; it comes within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider one on crypto. Second, in mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors, but by under a basis point: most of their advantage is information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs, and none of the representations tested extrapolates to unseen spread regimes. Third, a near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right: we show that such a comparator detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses, and confirm it in synthetic markets and on pendulums.

papers.title: TitanMPAS - a new global and regional Titan atmospheric circulation model. Part I: Global model results
papers.abstract: We developed TitanMPAS, a new Titan global and regional climate model, to simulate atmospheric dynamics and methane cycles. It integrates the non-hydrostatic MPAS dynamical core and TitanWRF physics parameterizations, with corrections to relax the thin-atmosphere assumptions on the gravity and curvature terms. TitanMPAS improves upon TitanWRF by incorporating a better moist convection parameterization and the observed surface properties. Long-term simulations ($>$100 Titan years) with a high resolution of $1^\circ$ and the realistic topography show that TitanMPAS is able to produce the stratospheric superrotation with typical equatorial wind speed over $\rm 120\,ms^{-1}$ and the maximum zonal wind speed exceeding $\rm 170\,ms^{-1}$ . Besides the good match of temperature profiles to the Cassini CIRS observations, the simulated wind, temperature and methane abundance in the troposphere match well with Huygens probe in-situ measurements. TitanMPAS also captures the major features of seasonal methane precipitation distribution patterns inferred from the observed cloud activities, as well as the vertical and latitudinal variations of methane abundance in the reanalysis of Cassini VIMS data. Resolution sensitivity studies show that higher resolution produces faster stratospheric superrotation, as well as stronger near-surface wind due to better resolved terrain variations. We further demonstrate that, despite the weak solar insolation, the near-surface temperature, pressure, wind magnitude and methane abundance all exhibit diurnal variations. Lastly, we show potential impacts of topography on methane transport and eddy momentum flux in both troposphere and stratosphere, which should be investigated in a future study.

papers.title: Adaptive Data Analysis and Adversarial Robustness on Insertion-Deletion Streams
papers.abstract: Classical streaming algorithms and statistical mechanisms frequently fail when future inputs or queries depend adaptively on prior outputs. In this work, we resolve central open questions in both adaptive data analysis (ADA) and adversarially robust turnstile streaming by introducing a unified hierarchical estimator-corrector-learner framework. For adaptive data analysis over an unrestricted domain, we design a randomized mechanism that answers $k$ adaptively chosen statistical queries to within additive error $\alpha$ using $\tilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha} + \frac{1}{\alpha^2})$ samples, nearly matching the lower bounds of Hardt and Ullman [FOCS 2014] and Steinke and Ullman [COLT 2015] while improving upon the classic $\tilde{O}(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha^2})$ bound of Dwork et al. [STOC 2015] and Bassily et al. [STOC 2016]. For known finite domains $U$, we combine our mechanism with private multiplicative weights to improve the sample complexity to $\tilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha^2}+ \min\left(\frac{\sqrt{k}}{\alpha}, \frac{\sqrt{\log |U|}}{\alpha^2}\right)\right)$. Building on our ADA mechanism, we construct a fixed linear sketch with a stateful decoder that answers $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ adaptive $F_2$ moment estimation queries to within a $(1\pm\epsilon)$-multiplicative factor using $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ bits of space. Finally, by embedding this sketch into a binary-tree recursion, we obtain the first nearly space-optimal adversarially robust algorithm for $F_2$ estimation on insertion-deletion streams. Our algorithm uses $\tilde O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ bits of space, improving upon the $\tilde{O}(\frac{1}{\epsilon^4})$ bound of Gribelyuk et al. [STOC 2026] and matching the insertion-only bound of Woodruff and Zhou [FOCS 2021]. This demonstrates that no asymptotic space overhead in $\epsilon$ is required to achieve adversarial robustness in the turnstile model.

papers.title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $\pi_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. Project page with code, data and videos: this https URL

papers.title: CPU Micro-Architectural Characteristic Sensitivity Study on CPU-Side Agentic Task Latency
papers.abstract: We perform a novel study of CPU micro-architectural characteristics on how they affect agentic AI CPU side latency. Small enterprises and individual users looking to reduce costs and seeking data privacy benefit from running agents locally, motivating an investigation into the optimal performance characteristics of an edge CPU to improve user experience. We investigate the relationship between CPU core frequency, CPU uncore frequency, active physical cores, and symmetric multi threading with agentic task latency in single and multi agent configurations. Across eight experiments on an Intel edge CPU, we find that P-core frequency produces the largest median latency improvement among the evaluated parameters. Increasing P-core frequency from 2.5 to 5.5 GHz yields a 1.154$\times$ speedup for a single agent and a 1.341$\times$ speedup for eight concurrent agents. We are the first to characterize hardware micro-architectural relationships on single and multi agent configurations with TerminalBench; we also provide an open source framework and dataset for repeatable CPU side latency agentic benchmarking.

papers.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Annealing for Protein Side-Chain Optimization: A Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical annealing solvers are moving from research laboratories toward industrial use, but their advantage over classical optimization appears to be confined to a narrow class of problems. A recent systematic benchmark of the D-Wave hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers, across several classes of optimization problems, found it to be most competitive on binary quadratic programs, while noting that few industrial problems take this form. Therefore, identifying real-world industrial problems that can be modeled with this structure is a key challenge. We propose protein side-chain optimization, a core step of computational protein design, as one of these problems: it is natively a binary quadratic program, and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. In this feasibility study, we test whether the competitiveness of the hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers extends to this problem. On 40 instances derived from 20 experimentally determined protein structures with up to about 200 amino acids and 2000 binary variables, we compare the results achieved with a hybrid solver, run for 5 seconds, against those of the commercial solver Gurobi, run for 10 seconds, 1000 seconds, and 4 hours. The hybrid solver reaches the certified optimum whenever one is available, matches Gurobi's performance on smaller instances, and outperforms it on larger instances, finding lower-energy solutions. These results show that the competitiveness of the hybrid solver on binary quadratic programs, so far observed only on a synthetic benchmark, extends to a real-world problem. This motivates comparisons with classical heuristics specific to protein side-chain optimization.

papers.title: FoleyForge: Free-form, Controllable, Rectified-flow Editing of Sound Effects
papers.abstract: We present FoleyForge, a generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects. Given an input clip and a free-form instruction describing the desired change, it applies the edit while preserving the input's identity. A single model handles semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like changes. We introduce a data pipeline that guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits, thus addressing the lack of publicly available audio editing data. Such data is then used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generation model, which we extend to expose attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance, yielding a more expressive editing model. FoleyForge achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.

papers.title: GeoRead: Geometry-Aware Transformer for Continuous AC-LGAD Readout Reconstruction
papers.abstract: AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (AC-LGADs) are promising silicon sensor technologies for high-precision four-dimensional tracking. Position reconstruction in AC-LGADs relies on correlations among waveforms induced on multiple readout pads, where analytically solving the signal propagation becomes difficult, motivating data-based machine learning reconstruction. Existing machine learning approaches generally assume a fixed readout pad layout and predict one hit from an isolated, temporally aligned waveform window. These assumptions limit their flexibility across sensor designs and applicability to continuous readout where signal arrival times are not known in advance and multiple hits might overlap in the same waveforms. We introduce GeoRead, a spatial-temporal Transformer enabling multi-event continuous position prediction and uncertainty estimation. We incorporate relative pad positions into attention and produces time-resolved hit position estimates with predictive uncertainties. Time-jitter and additive event-mixing augmentations are used to train the model on temporally misaligned and overlapping waveforms synthesized from single-event measurements. Using four-channel transient-current-technique (TCT) data of a 500\mum-pitch AC-LGAD, GeoRead achieves median position errors of 5.8\mum within the convex hull of the readout-pad centers and 8.2\mum over the full scanned region at 190\volt. The model maintains comparable accuracy under temporal shifts and demonstrates time-resolved reconstruction of superposed events, without predefined per-event window. These results provide a basis for extending waveform-based position reconstruction toward continuous readout and flexible sensor geometries.

papers.title: Enabling Retraining-Free Accurate Inference in Analog Compute in Memory Accelerators
papers.abstract: Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators compute matrix-vector products directly inside memory arrays, eliminating weight movement and promising order-of-magnitude gains in inference efficiency. However, converter and device errors make pretrained models unusable on these arrays, and hardware-aware retraining is costly. We enable retraining-free, accurate inference of pretrained models on simple analog arrays with low-cost, shared calibration. Our key observation is that analog error depends on how each layer is represented on the array, and that this representation can be changed offline without changing the computation. We center the inputs and apply Hadamard rotations designed for analog arrays, which keep shared reference errors spread and confine input mixing to each array. Across CNNs, vision transformers and LLMs up to 14B parameters on PCM and ReRAM, the method brings vision models and larger LLMs within a few points of floating-point accuracy and matches or approaches published hardware-aware training without training any weights. On ReRAM with 6-bit ADCs, it restores ViT-B/16 from 37.4% to 82.9% and Phi-4 from 27.0% to 72.2%, both within 2.2 points of floating-point accuracy.

papers.title: Stability of large dynamical systems using Gershgorin Disc Theorem
papers.abstract: Understanding the stability of large nonlinear dynamical systems is a fundamental problem in many fields, including biological, technological, and social networks. Traditional stability methods often rely on explicit eigenvalue calculations or the construction of Lyapunov functions, which become computationally difficult for large interconnected systems. In this work, we introduce a stability classifier that provides a computationally efficient way to determine the stability of complex systems without performing full spectral analysis. Our approach combines the Dynamical Jacobian Ensemble framework, which uses the network structure and the underlying dynamics to construct a Jacobian, with the Gershgorin disc theorem, which provides bounds on the eigenvalues of the system's Jacobian matrix. Using this combination, we derive an analytical classifier that predicts whether a dynamical system is asymptotically stable, unstable, or sensitively stable based on a small set of dynamical and network parameters. The analysis reveals that the stability of large dynamical systems is strongly influenced by highly connected hub nodes. This observation allows the stability condition to be simplified by focusing on the contribution of the hub-associated Gershgorin disc. Extensive numerical simulations on large ensembles of Jacobian matrices confirm that the proposed classifier accurately separates stable, unstable, and sensitively stable regimes across a wide range of dynamical parameters and network structures. The resulting framework provides a simple and scalable tool for predicting the stability of large dynamical networks while capturing the interplay between network topology and interaction dynamics.

papers.title: The quaternionic reflection groups with imprimitive complexifications and the finite subgroups of GL(2,C)
papers.abstract: We give a transparent development of the quaternionic reflection groups which have imprimitive complexifications, including a description of their reflections and the corresponding normal reflection subgroups. They are seen to be of rank one or rank two, and are obtained from minimal complex reflection groups by the addition of one quaternionic reflection and a complex scalar matrix of finite order. In the case of the rank two groups, we use our techniques to consider the broader question of what are the minimal irreducible subgroups of GL(2,C) with a given collineation group. This leads to a complete classification of the finite irreducible subgroups of GL(2,C) in terms of the minimal groups, with the groups giving rise to quaternionic reflection groups located within it.

papers.title: Exact and hybrid neutrino oscillation probabilities via the evolution operator
papers.abstract: We revisit the three-flavor neutrino oscillations in constant-density matter using the evolution matrix expressed in terms of the Lagrange-Sylvester interpolation. Taking advantage of Vieta's formulas for the Hamiltonian of the system, we derive exact closed expressions for the oscillation probabilities $P_{ee}$, $P_{\mu e}$, and $P_{\mu\tau}$, which are concise and simple, and structurally identical to their vacuum counterparts. The CP-violation contribution, proportional to the Jarlskog invariant $\mathcal{J}$, appears as a single, clearly separated term. Our approach does not require introducing neutrino mixing in the medium and avoids using a matter-dependent CP-violation phase, facilitating the separation of genuine CP violation from that induced by matter effects. We explicitly verify that, in the limit $V \to 0$, our expressions for the flavor transition probabilities reduce to the well-known vacuum formulas. The exact structure of the probabilities is preserved if the exact, not very enlightening, trigonometric eigenvalues are replaced by approximate expressions in radicals. We illustrate this hybrid approach with eigenvalues obtained from two successive rotations of the Hamiltonian. For an experiment like DUNE, the hybrid probability values match those of the exact probabilities within absolute errors of about $2\times 10^{-6}$ in all channels and relative errors less than $0.01 \%$ for $P_{ee}$, $P_{\mu e}$, and $P_{\mu\tau}$.

papers.title: A Gamma-Mixture Solution for Definite Noncentral Complex Gaussian Quadratic Forms
papers.abstract: Finding exact solutions for the statistics of definite noncentral complex Gaussian quadratic forms (CGQFs) has long been a challenging problem. Among existing exact approaches, Raphaeli's formulation [1] remains the most computationally efficient. However, its analytical tractability is hindered by the dependence of its series coefficients on the evaluation variable, which confines their statistics to the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF). This paper overcomes this limitation by deriving novel Gamma-mixture representations for the PDF and CDF of positive- and negative-definite noncentral CGQFs. The resulting structure broadens Raphaeli's statistical framework beyond the PDF and CDF to a wider class of CGQF functionals and a substantial range of practical applications. In particular, expectations of integrable functions of definite noncentral CGQFs are expressed as weighted sums of the corresponding expectations over Gamma random variables, enabling the direct derivation of moments, transforms, and performance measures. Moreover, the proposed formulation reduces the single-point complexity from \(O\!\left(n^2K+nK^2\right)\) for Raphaeli's method to \(O\!\left(nK+K^2\right)\), where \(n\) denotes the quadratic-form dimension and \(K\) the truncation order. The proposed Gamma-mixture structure also enables closed-form approximations that, by construction, remain valid probability distributions for any truncation order. In addition, uniform PDF and CDF truncation-error bounds are derived, allowing prescribed-accuracy truncation. As a sample application, we derive the first reported exact average bit error rate expression for maximal-ratio combining receivers with an arbitrary number of branches under an arbitrary positive-definite Rician correlation structure.

papers.title: Regularity of Weak Solutions near Singular Minimizing Cones for the One-Phase Free Boundary Problem
papers.abstract: Alt and Caffarelli proved an Allard-type $\epsilon$-regularity theorem near the flat one-homogeneous minimizer of the one-phase free boundary problem. A natural follow-up question is whether an analogous regularity result holds near singular minimizing cones. In this paper, we prove such an $\epsilon$-regularity theorem near a strongly integrable one-phase minimizing cone with an isolated singularity. More precisely, we show that, after a suitable translation and rotation, the free boundary of any non-degenerate weak solution sufficiently close to the cone is graphical over the free boundary of a leaf of the De Silva--Jerison--Shahgholian foliation. This result is analogous to recent $\epsilon$-regularity theorems in minimal surface theory by Edelen and by Edelen--Spolaor; our proof adapts the strategy of Edelen to the one-phase setting.

papers.title: McShane's identity and the Brownian loop measure
papers.abstract: We combine McShane's identity for a once-punctured torus with the length-spectrum identity of Wang and Xue. An exact identity in each primitive homology class yields a finite limit for the difference of two divergent length-spectrum sums over self-intersecting hyperbolic geodesics. The limit is $\frac18$ and is equivalent to McShane's identity. We also derive higher-iteration identities governed by integer divisors.

papers.title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods for Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence via Increment Sharing
papers.abstract: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.

papers.title: Fibered Separation Logic: Weakest Preconditions, Universal Constructions, and Local Independence
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a categorical framework for models of higher-order separation logic including the weakest precondition modality. Weakest preconditions are interpreted by strong monads on a category fibered over a model of Moggi's computational lambda calculus. The fibered categories in question are termed bunched fibrations and shown to be equivalent to BI hyperdoctrines. Well-known heuristic techniques for obtaining weakest preconditions are shown to be expressible in categorical terms and are proved sound. The ``baking in the frame rule'' trick is shown to satisfy a universal property. Constructions are given for extending a program logic with cost credits. Our largest case study is parametrized by a category having local independent product (LIP) structure, a notion due to Simpson that axiomatizes name generation, randomness, and local state. From an LIP category, we construct an allocation monad, a bunched fibration, and a monad lifting. We instantiate our construction to obtain a novel probabilistic separation logic for measure-theoretic probability that both simplifies and clarifies prior work.

papers.title: Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine
papers.abstract: Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.

papers.title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings. We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.

papers.title: Transporting the Past: An Optimal Transport View of Backtracking Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: We study backtracking counterfactual inference for Structural Causal Models (SCMs) through the lens of optimal transport. In SCMs, a factual observation generally induces a posterior distribution over exogenous variables, making counterfactual inference inherently distributional. We introduce two complementary frameworks that transport this posterior onto the set of exogenous configurations satisfying a desired counterfactual query. The first constructs a natural pointwise projection and is suitable when the transported exogenous distribution can be used directly. The second enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables, so that the transported variables remain interpretable as genuine exogenous noises of the same SCM. We show that both frameworks are consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle, and we propose marginal, penalty-based, and hard-constrained solvers for finite-posterior settings. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the geometry of the problem and reveal trade-offs among transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.

papers.title: National and State-Level Approaches to Automated Vehicle Certification: A Comparative Framework for State Operational Governance
papers.abstract: Automated vehicle (AV) deployment in the United States is expanding without a unified federal certification framework, leading to substantial variation in how states authorize and oversee AV testing and deployment. This paper examines how U.S. states regulate Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) Level 4-5 automated driving systems (ADS), identifies common certification approaches, compares them with international practices, and evaluates the implications for North Carolina's future regulatory strategy. Publicly available state statutes, administrative regulations, agency guidance, and federal policy documents were reviewed. Ten states, selected to capture the range of regulatory approaches, were analyzed using a structured framework covering operational scope, governance and oversight, federal interaction, and implementation outcomes. Certification practices in the European Union, China, Japan, and Australia were reviewed for comparative context. Three state certification models were identified, reflecting increasing regulatory involvement: baseline legal compliance, administrative self-certification with ongoing oversight, and permit-based authorization requiring formal agency review before deployment. North Carolina currently aligns with the baseline compliance model. International frameworks are converging toward scenario-based testing, operational-design-domain-specific approval, safety-case documentation, cybersecurity assurance, and lifecycle oversight, although direct transferability to the U.S. is limited. The paper develops a three-model typology for comparing state AV certification approaches and integrates state practices with international frameworks, providing a consistent basis for evaluating differences in regulatory involvement, governance complexity, and institutional responsibilities across jurisdictions.

papers.title: A Phase-Transition Portal to Enhanced Dark Matter Annihilation
papers.abstract: We present a thermal dark matter (DM) scenario in which a phase transition after freeze-out changes both the DM spectrum and the dominant annihilation process, allowing an enhanced present day annihilation rate with suppressed direct detection. We realize this mechanism in a two-Higgs-doublet model extended by a complex scalar singlet, a Majorana fermion, and a heavier Dirac fermion. Before the transition, the Majorana state freezes out through $p$-wave annihilation into singlet scalars. The subsequent transition changes the dark fermion masses and mixing, enabling $s$-wave annihilation through a pseudoscalar portal. The surviving relic differs in mass and composition from the original state. We find relic compatible solutions with present day annihilation rates more than an order of magnitude above the canonical thermal value, without tuning to a mediator resonance, while satisfying direct detection bounds.

papers.title: Special line bundles on tetragonal curves
papers.abstract: One can associate a pair of vector bundles $(E, F)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ to every tetragonal curve: $E$ is the Tschirnhausen bundle and $F$ records numerical data of the ideal for the curve under its relative canonical embedding. In this note, we show that a Hurwitz--Brill--Noether general tetragonal curve must have balanced $E$, $F$ bundles, and provide counterexamples for the converse when $g = 8$ or $g \geq 10$.

papers.title: Jackknife-conformal uncertainty for linear ACE potentials: calibrated forces and silicon properties compared with Bayesian and POPS baselines
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials are misspecified, so Bayesian posterior variances understate their errors. For linear atomic cluster expansion (ACE) potentials we derive calibrated uncertainties from one misspecification-robust parameter covariance, the delete-one-configuration jackknife. Scaled by one conformal quantile from a held-out part of the training set, it gives per-atom force uncertainties close to their target coverage on held-out silicon data and on cracks left out of the fit; screw dislocations left out are under-covered by the smaller of the two models. With one scale fitted to the forces of a held-out test split, the same parameter distribution is propagated to 21 properties of silicon, from elastic constants to defect and surface energies, by implicit differentiation through each relaxation and by committees, and is tested against density functional theory (DFT) without tuning on any property. For a smaller and a larger model the intervals cover most properties, and the larger model's are about 4 times tighter. The Bayesian posterior with one calibrated scale has the wrong shape: it covers fewer properties and has far lower joint evidence. Pointwise optimal parameter sets (POPS), once their hypercube is numerically defined, performs comparably on the properties, but its per-atom force regions are not calibrated to a target (0.95 and 0.84 at a nominal 0.90). Where the jackknife fails is relaxed point defects, whose training cells are all hot snapshots: a bias that every configuration shares is invisible to a jackknife, but it can be measured from the training labels, and as a discrepancy term, devised after the property results were seen, it brings the coverage close to nominal.

papers.title: Thirty years of 2D MIT
papers.abstract: The zero-magnetic-field metal-insulator transition in strongly correlated two-dimensional electron systems was experimentally discovered three decades ago, thereby triggering extensive experimental and theoretical investigations. Prior to this discovery, the occurrence of such a transition --- as well as the very existence of a metallic phase in two dimensions --- was regarded as forbidden within the framework of the one-parameter scaling theory of localization. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of the transport and thermodynamic properties of two-dimensional electron and hole systems in which carrier-carrier interactions constitute the dominant energy scale. We present and critically analyze both experimental observations and theoretical developments accumulated over the past thirty years.

papers.title: Expanding the Volatile Abundance Inventory for High-Priority K-Dwarf JWST Exoplanet Systems
papers.abstract: There are exceedingly few chemical abundance measurements available in the literature for K dwarf stars, especially for those with T$_{eff} <$ 4700 K due to an incompatibility of traditional analyses with their molecular-line-ridden optical spectra. To address the need for K dwarf abundance constraints, we present an elemental ([C/H], [O/H]) and isotopic ($^{12}$C/$^{13}$C, $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O) abundance analysis for six K dwarf exoplanet host stars: K2-141, NGTS-10, WASP-43, WASP-69, WASP-80, and HATS-72. Each system hosts an exoplanet targeted by JWST characterization efforts, making host star abundances especially critical as baseline references. Using MARCS model atmospheres, the TurboSpectrum spectral synthesis code, and near-infrared IGRINS spectra, we derive novel [C/H] and [O/H] abundance ratios for these high-priority K dwarf host stars. We further investigate prospects for determining $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C and $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios using $^{13}$C$^{16}$O and $^{12}$C$^{18}$O lines from the 2.3 micron CO bandhead. The observed spectra are too noisy to measure $^{16}$O/$^{18}$O ratios for the sample, but we do find sub-solar $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratios for five out of six targets. We also derive uniform gyrochronological ages for each host star to compare with galactic chemical evolution models and identify underlying abundance-age trends. NIR H+K band spectroscopy provides an alternative to optical, atomic line-derived carbon and oxygen abundances for cool dwarf stars. The growing catalog of precise host star elemental and isotopic abundances complements ongoing observations of their companions and provides a baseline for understanding their chemical composition, origin, and evolution.

papers.title: A Complete Calculus for Hamiltonian Quantum Programming
papers.abstract: Given the forces acting on a quantum particle, a Hamiltonian models its continuous evolution. Quantum computers evolve Hamiltonians to simulate physical systems, to solve optimisation problems, and to estimate eigenvalues, and even the popular circuit abstraction is compiled to Hamiltonians on the hardware. We introduce Hamilton, a process calculus whose parallel operator is the sum of interactions acting simultaneously. Its operational semantics is the Lie-Trotter product formula, which recovers a sum as the limit of ever finer sequential interleavings; compiling a program means halving it to a chosen precision and unrolling the interleaving into a circuit. The semantics is fully abstract, the expressible Hamiltonians are exactly those whose Pauli coefficients have the form $m/2^k$, the precision that successive halving reaches, and the equational theory is complete and decidable. A full implementation compiles Hamilton programs to circuits and decides their equivalence, and Agda proofs sanity-check the core metatheory.

papers.title: Counting Finite Maps through Functional Digraphs and Fibers
papers.abstract: We count solutions of composition identities for maps on finite sets, first for three identities in which both maps vary and then for commutation with a prescribed arithmetic map. For $f\circ g=f\circ g\circ g$, drawing an arrow from each element to its image reduces the enumeration to rooted trees attached to directed cycles. For $f\circ f=f\circ g\circ f$, grouping elements with the same $f$-value leads instead to a partition-based enumeration. A classical rooted-forest enumeration leads in both problems to $\mathcal T(x)$, the exponential generating function for rooted labeled trees. For $f=g\circ f\circ g$, the values on the cycles of $g$ determine all remaining values. The exponential generating function $\mathcal D$ for these ordered pairs and the ordinary generating function $\mathcal A$ for endofunctions up to relabeling satisfy $\mathcal D(x)=\mathcal A(\mathcal T(x))$. Finally, we count functions on $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ satisfying $f(ax)=af(x)$, first for prime multipliers $a$ and then for a broader class of composite multipliers. In each problem, fixing one map exposes independent choices for the other through its functional digraph or its fibers.

papers.title: Optimal Contention Resolution from Samples
papers.abstract: Contention resolution schemes convert random sets which are ex-ante feasible for some constraint into sets which are feasible ex post, and their online variants have broad applications in Bayesian and stochastic optimization, including prophet inequalities and stochastic probing. In many such applications, however, full distributional knowledge is an unattainable requirement. This motivates the study of contention resolution schemes which employ a limited number of samples from the underlying distributions. We study sample-based contention resolution for $k$-uniform matroids, for both uniformly random and adversarial arrival orders, and compare their balance guarantees to the best possible with full distributional knowledge. For a single-item constraint, we show that one sample per element suffices for an optimal $(1-1/e)$-balanced ROCRS. For adversarial arrivals, however, we prove that no single-sample OCRS can be $1/2$-balanced, even for known arrival orders, separating contention resolution from prophet inequalities in the single-sample setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that two samples are necessary and sufficient for the optimal $1/2$ guarantee. We also present a single-sample $0.48$-balanced scheme. For general $k$, we give a simple single-sample ROCRS that achieves an optimal balance ratio of $1-e^{-k}k^k/k!$. In adversarial order, we obtain a single-sample $(1 - O(1/\sqrt{k}))$-balanced scheme, matching the optimal asymptotic dependence on $k$. Finally, we complete the picture by characterizing the minimum number of samples needed to match the optimal balance ratio achievable with full distributional knowledge. For random arrivals, one sample suffices for $k = 1,2,3,4$, and zero samples suffice for $k \geq 5$. For an adversarial arrival order, even known in advance, and any $k \geq 2$, we show that no constant number of samples suffices to achieve optimal balance.

papers.title: Real-World Adoption, Use, and Governance of an LLM-Based Electronic Health Record Search and Synthesis Platform
papers.abstract: We evaluated the longitudinal adoption and use of Scout, an electronic health record-integrated large language model platform that provides cited search and synthesis of patient records, during staged deployment across a multi-hospital academic health system. Over 11 months, 2,635 users completed 80,465 tasks. 1,768 clinical users initiated use within the first 29 days of system-wide launch, which included a required training. Daily initiation increased 21.2-fold at launch, from 2.9 to 61.0 users per day. Of the 495 users who initiated use during the launch week, 310 did so in the first two days. Use spanned more than 20 recorded specialty categories, five care-practitioner roles, and 46,485 distinct prompts involving retrieval, synthesis, extraction, evaluation, and drafting, with 752 tasks saved for reuse. Among care practitioners who completed the required course, 77.9% went on to use Scout, with a median of 1.7 days after course completion. The highest-intensity user quintile accounted for 59.0% of tasks and 61.9% of tokens. Exploratory prompt analysis showed use across retrieval, synthesis, extraction, evaluation, and note-drafting. These findings suggest that rapid, broad adoption requires clinician-led task design and evaluation, traceable governance proportional to reach, centralized capacity planning and user support, and training integrated with access.

papers.title: Greedy Byte-Pair Encoding Achieves at Least 0.361 of the Optimal Compression
papers.abstract: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) builds a tokeniser by repeatedly merging a most frequent adjacent pair of symbols; its utility is the total reduction in string length achieved by $k$ merges. It was known that this greedy rule achieves at least a third of the optimal reduction. We prove that it always achieves at least 0.361 of the optimal reduction in string length, for every string, every budget and every tie-breaking rule; this is the first improvement of the bound one third. We also explain why one third was a barrier: the pair-packing relaxation behind it is tight, so a better bound must use more of the optimum's structure. When greedy destroys three of the optimum's merge points at once, one of them can usually be moved next door, because all copies of a rule of the optimum look alike; the remaining cases are paid for later. Along the way we determine the worst-case ratio for two merges exactly, bound it for three, and isolate a single inequality that would settle the problem.

papers.title: Non-conical classical solutions to the one-phase free boundary problem with an isolated singularity
papers.abstract: Several examples of one-homogeneous classical solutions to the one-phase free boundary problem with an isolated free boundary singularity are known. Adapting the approach of Caffarelli, Hardt, and Simon for minimal surfaces, we construct non-conical classical solutions with an isolated free boundary singularity by perturbing a one-homogeneous solution $U$. Moreover, if $U$ is strictly stable (respectively, non-degenerate), then any solution sufficiently close to $U$ is also strictly stable (respectively, non-degenerate).

papers.title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.

papers.title: Standard Subspaces and Modular Theory -- General Theory and Applications to QFT
papers.abstract: This is a preview of an upcoming monograph on standard subspaces and modular theory. At the moment, it consists of the first chapter. This starts with a gentle introduction to the subject, and then describes the modular theory of standard subspaces, the characterization of their modular data by the KMS condition and reflection positivity, and various constructions of standard subspaces. Further topics in Chapter 1 include the connection of standard subspaces to complexifications and symplectic structures, including their polarizers, and operations with standard subspaces, namely direct sums, direct integrals, and tensor products. Many examples and classification results are included as well. This first chapter also contains a description of the free U(1)-current and some other applications to quantum field theory, such as KMS states of type I factors, the local subspaces of the free Klein--Gordon field, and the entropy operator defined by a standard subspace.

papers.title: Devitrification: crystal nucleation and growth mechanisms in glasses
papers.abstract: If a liquid is cooled rapidly, it may fall out of equilibrium before it can crystallize. It may, however, crystallize later from the nonequilibrium glassy state. Using the Random First-Order Transition (RFOT) theory of glasses, we discuss a variety of mechanisms of crystallization as a route to devitrification. Ordinary nucleation is sped up by the frozen in energy of the glass relative to the liquid. At sufficiently low temperatures, a mechanism of nanonucleation appears, producing nanometer scale crystal inclusions in the glass. Nanocrystallization depends strongly on the local fluctuations in stability, and the transition from classical nucleation and growth to nanocrystallization occurs dominantly through rare, less stable glassy regions that percolate through space, producing an additional dramatic speedup in the crystal nucleation and growth rates. Similar fluctuations in local stability also explain anomalies of crystal growth in deeply supercooled systems.

papers.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
papers.abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.

papers.title: Dynamic GPU Voxel Grids and Voxel-sequential Processing in NanoVDB
papers.abstract: We introduce two fundamental advances to the NanoVDB data structure: dynamic GPU-native topological updates, and a voxel-sequential access paradigm that dramatically accelerates point-wise and stencil-based operators on sparse grids. NanoVDB's linearized memory layout has delivered strong GPU performance, and the Index-Grid concept introduced in the fVDB framework [Williams et al 2024] provided topology/data separation and optimal compactness of storage in sparse machine learning workloads. However, all these prior iterations of NanoVDB assume a static topology that has precluded use of this data structure in simulation and dynamic geometric processes. We eliminate this limitation by introducing a suite of dynamic topology operators -- morphological dilation, grid merging, pruning, and cross-resolution coarsening and refinement. These operators use bit-parallel algorithms to reconstruct grids containing hundreds of millions of voxels in just a few milliseconds. We also introduce a voxel-sequential access paradigm and data structure for GPU kernels operating on sparse data. We stream active voxels as a flat linear sequence, minimizing or eliminating the need for tree traversal in the process. This achieves compute density and regularity that allow even complex stencil-based operators to approach peak memory bandwidth, with minimal storage overhead. Together, these contributions remove the read-only constraint from NanoVDB, establishing it as a high-performance primary representation for dynamic GPU simulation and geometry manipulation. We evaluate the efficacy of our newly introduced operators in benchmarks sourced from applications such as 3D reconstruction, fluid simulation, and large-scale mesh voxelization.

papers.title: ForPC: Force-Aware Whole-Body Control for Precise Humanoid Cart Pushing
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are expected to take over strenuous material handling in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, where operating existing wheeled carts would let them move heavy loads without modifying the workplace. However, humanoid cart pushing remains challenging because the bimanual grasp closes a force-coupled loop in which the contact wrenches that drive the cart also disturb the robot's balance, and payload changes alter the coupled dynamics. We propose ForPC, a force-aware whole-body control framework that regulates cart velocity through two-stage reinforcement learning. A locomotion prior is first trained under varied hand loads and upper-body postures to provide balance support. A force latent and a state latent are then inferred from onboard observations, without external force sensors, and fed to a residual policy that coordinates bounded arm, waist, and leg adjustments with base-velocity commands. Multi-objective rewards penalize bimanual internal opposition, grasp slip, and actuator saturation, encouraging the policy to apply contact force on demand without human demonstrations. Sim-to-sim experiments show that ForPC reduces cart-velocity RMSE by up to 68.2% relative to a locomotion-only baseline (Loco-only) and cross-track RMSE by up to 74.2% on the multi-bend route. Trained solely in simulation, the policy also transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without real-world training or fine-tuning and, with no payload-specific adjustment, pushes a cart carrying up to 30 kg at 0.5 m/s. These results suggest that humanoid robots could eventually replace humans for efficient material handling in daily life.

papers.title: Disentangling Multiple Scaling Dimensions via Operator Covariance in Critical Quantum Spin Systems
papers.abstract: We present a general proof of different power-law decays versus distance of the eigenvalues of two-point covariance matrices in critical lattice quantum models, allowing extraction of multiple scaling dimensions. We demonstrate the practical utility of this method in the context of a spin-1/2 chain with critical ground state described by the SU(2)_1 Wess--Zumino--Witten field theory. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations to compute covariance matrices in different symmetry sectors, we resolve the expected relevant and marginal primary operators as well as some descendants. The covariance method can be integrated into many existing numerical schemes and promises to significantly enhance computational studies of quantum criticality.

papers.title: Blow-Up and Life-Span for Nonlinear Hardy-Hénon Parabolic Equations
papers.abstract: We consider the nonlinear Hardy-Hénon parabolic equation $ u_t=\Delta u+|x|^l|u|^\alpha u,$ $t>0,$ $x\in\mathbb{R}^N$ or $x\in\mathbb{R}^N\setminus\{0\}$, with $N\ge1$, $l>-\min\{2,N\}$, $\alpha>0$, with nonnegative initial datum $u_0$. We first establish new criteria for finite-time blow-up. We then derive optimal upper bounds for the life-span $T_{\max}(\lambda\varphi)$ of solutions arising from the initial datum $u_0=\lambda\varphi$. These estimates establish a precise dependence of $T_{\max}(\lambda\varphi)$ on both the initial profile $\varphi$ and the parameter $\lambda$ in the small and large-amplitude regimes.

papers.title: Liouville transforms for ordinary differential equations with distributional coefficients
papers.abstract: We study Liouville transforms for the differential equation $Ju'+qu=wf$ on the real interval $(a,b)$ where $J$ is a constant, invertible, skew-hermitian matrix and $q$ and $w$ are matrices whose entries are distributions of order $0$ with $q$ Hermitian and $w$ non-negative. In particular, we examine their use in the treatment of quasi-regular endpoints and their impact on the Weyl-Titchmarsh $\mathbb M$-function associated with the differential equation.

papers.title: AutoParallel: Composable, PyTorch-Native Automatic Parallelism for Production Training
papers.abstract: Training large models requires multiple interacting forms of parallelism. As models and clusters scale, finding and maintaining efficient parallelization plans becomes essential for training performance. Diverse model architectures, workloads, and hardware topologies demand flexible strategies, yet production PyTorch systems typically rely on hand-written recipes that are costly to adapt and tend to reuse familiar patterns, which may be suboptimal for a given workload. We present AutoParallel, a PyTorch-native planner for distributed model training. AutoParallel searches parallelization choices jointly across the training computation, allowing established techniques to be combined and unconventional strategies to emerge. It expresses its decisions using native PyTorch abstractions and produces ordinary PyTorch programs, avoiding a separate execution runtime while composing directly with the PyTorch compilation and training stack. AutoParallel also composes automatic decisions with model-specific distributed code, allowing dynamic or specialized regions to remain under user control. Plans are inspectable and replayable artifacts. Across dense, hybrid, and mixture-of-experts models on meshes of up to four dimensions and 128 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, AutoParallel matches or exceeds expert-written TorchTitan recipes on most configurations, with throughput gains of up to 18.3%, and discovers plans that uniform expert recipes do not express.

papers.title: The Re-Foundation of Radar Meteorology
papers.abstract: Since the early development of radar meteorology in the 1940s, rainfall retrieval has traditionally relied on empirical scaling relationships between radar variables and rainfall rate. Here, we revisit the premise that horizontal and differential reflectivity sufficiently constrain the rainfall rate despite the variability of the underlying drop size distribution. Motivated by evidences that this variability requires at least three degrees of freedom, we develop a nonparametric statistical retrieval algorithm that considers different combinations of drop count and distribution shape compatible with the same radar observations. The method separates the contributions of drop count and distribution shape. It then empirically estimates how the shape factors for rainfall rate and horizontal reflectivity, as well as differential reflectivity, vary with the mean and skewness of the drop diameter distribution. These relationships identify compatible combinations of drop count and shape, from which rainfall rates are calculated and their median returned as the estimate. Neither a prescribed analytical drop size distribution nor a scaling rainfall estimator or explicit classification of precipitation regimes is required. We evaluate the method using a worldwide database (149 disdrometer datasets from 76 locations), with radar observables calculated from measured drop spectra. In cross-dataset validation, the method achieves lower median dispersion of relative retrieval errors across all 16 combinations of training and validation instrument types with respect two benchmark methods consisting of the traditional scaling law relationship, and a direct nonparametric fit. These findings motivate a reassessment of the foundations of radar rainfall retrieval by incorporating the range of rainfall rates compatible with radar observation.

papers.title: Physical Sensing Verification for Cognitive ISAC against UAV Spoofing via Digital Twins
papers.abstract: As integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) lets 5G and 6G base stations detect drones, software agents will soon act on what they sense. This amplifies the threat of a relay replaying the base station's signal as a phantom drone. For such cognitive ISAC systems, this paper proposes a wall-based physical check. A digital twin (DT) predicts where a real target's wall echo must arrive; a relay can fake range, but not where its own reflections come from. The paper proves that line-of-sight beam steering cannot expose a matched relay, and that, under stated conditions, a single-antenna relay faking a wall echo leaves a telltale echo where a genuine target leaves none. In a pre-registered ray-tracing study, the twin's evidence separated genuine targets from replays perfectly (AUC 1.000) on held-out streets, and a later-registered passive check needing no extra transmission accepted every genuine target and no replay. The primary active probe was inconclusive, at 5.3\% false acceptances against a 5\% limit, for lack of threshold margin. At the evaluated relay positions, the conditional bound certifies 3 of 24 held-out streets, reproduced on fresh ones, against single-antenna relay signals meeting its conditions, adaptive or fixed, and 11 of 24 at double bandwidth.

papers.title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
papers.abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.

papers.title: Higher Order Component Attribution via Learned Surrogates in High Energy Physics
papers.abstract: Experimental High Energy Physics (HEP) has adopted the transformer architecture for identification of jets, particularly the state-of-the-art Particle Transformer (ParT) which injects explicit information about particle correlations into the attention mechanism. While able to achieve state-of-the-art results in accuracy, interpretability to its effectiveness has been limited. In this paper we propose component attribution methods using Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) that directly tie back to the physical descriptors of jets, to probe whether mechanisms such as Multi-Head Attention (MHA), or the ParT architecture, are able to learn these as discriminating features.

papers.title: Scoring, Not Learning: Decomposing Catalog-Consolidation Gains in Web-Scraped Retail Product Recognition
papers.abstract: Retail product catalogs assembled from web image search are cheap to build and pervasively noisy: queries return packaging shots instead of products, and entries proliferate under names that cannot be distinguished visually. Consolidating such a catalog can look like an alternative to scaling the model. We show this is not a comparison between two ways of improving a recognizer, but between improving a recognizer and changing what counts as correct. We study a public archive of 165,769 cheese images across 1,824 query-named entries. A packaging filter and near-duplicate removal reduce it to a 998-class recognition set on one fixed, group-aware split. Canonicalizing entries to their base type (844 classes) raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. Scoring the unchanged model against the merged label space, by summing its predicted probability within each canonical group, recovers +4.27 points with no retraining (+4.25 over six seeds). Retraining on the consolidated catalog then adds -0.10$\pm$0.53, +0.08$\pm$0.65 and -0.10$\pm$0.65 points at 28, 50 and 88 M parameters, indistinguishable from zero at every capacity ($\pm$ is the across-seed standard deviation). That component is specific, not mechanical: random merges with the identical size profile yield only +0.68 points, and the three backbones agree to within 0.1 points. But it is overwhelmingly category coarsening, not alias correction: across the 37 merged groups, type coarsenings supply 94% of the gain and alias collapses only 7%.
